summary: Discusses issues to consider when choosing the underlying communications services for an SNMP implementation. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: This is advice on how network monitoring messages should travel.

questions: what communications services can snmp use
subtitle: An argument for running SNMP over UDP/IP rather than directly on a data link or over a connection-oriented transport.

tldr.problem: Several memos described ways to carry SNMP over other protocols than UDP, which caused confusion about what an implementor should choose.
tldr.mechanism: The memo weighs transport and network layers against raw data links, and connectionless against connection-oriented transport, and concludes that SNMP over UDP/IP is best apart from a few special circumstances.
tldr.outcome: It is an Informational discussion, not a standard. It says only SNMP over UDP is standardized, so use UDP/IP on the Internet and native services elsewhere.

facts.label: Minimal UDP/IP stack example
facts.value: under 4Kb of code, about two months

today: RFC 1270 is an Informational memo and has not been obsoleted or updated. It records the reasoning for SNMP over UDP at the time (1991), and it does not define a standard.

sections.title: Why the Question Came Up
sections.content:
RFC 1270 discusses what to consider when choosing the communications services under an SNMP implementation. It explains that the Internet's network management framework rests on the Structure of Management Information (RFC 1155), the Management Information Base (RFC 1156) and the Simple Network Management Protocol (RFC 1157).

Other memos had been published on carrying SNMP over Ethernet, OSI and IPX, and they confused the community. The memo notes that only the SNMP specification is an Internet Standard. SNMP over OSI and over Ethernet are Experimental, and SNMP over IPX was an Internet Draft. It does not present a standard or protocol itself.
sections.plainLanguage: People invented several different ways to deliver monitoring messages, and nobody knew which to pick. This note helps choose.

sections.title: Standardization and Interoperability
sections.content:
The SNMP specification names only UDP for exchanging SNMP messages. To claim full compliance, an implementation has to use UDP. The IAB might standardize others later, but only UDP is currently standardized.

The memo reasons that the Internet is the largest market for SNMP systems, so its needs will drive SNMP. A device that must operate and be managed on the Internet on a production basis must support SNMP over UDP/IP. That will make it the most common method, and so give the widest interoperability and acceptance.
sections.plainLanguage: If everyone speaks the same language, everyone understands each other. UDP is the language the Internet already speaks.

sections.title: To Transport or Not to Transport
sections.content:
The memo prefers running SNMP over a transport and network protocol stack, not directly on the data link. It lists five functions these give: routing (management continues around failed areas), media independence, an end-to-end checksum, multiplexing and demultiplexing, and fragmentation and reassembly. Fragmentation lowers robustness, since losing one fragment fails the operation, so small packets should be used when the network is operating poorly.

The usual objections are development time and resources, and the memo calls them less than compelling. It says a minimal UDP/IP stack it knows of took less than 4Kb of code space and about two months for one person. The UDP/IP header takes 28 octets with no IP options, and UDP adds no overhead traffic of its own. SNMP over a data link cannot traverse a router.

Running directly on the data link is reasonable in some cases: dedicated out-of-band point-to-point or dial-up links, and a data link interface that must be manageable independent of the higher protocol suite.
sections.plainLanguage: Using the full postal system lets a message find its way around roadblocks and across towns. Using only the street outside your house does not.

sections.title: Connectionless Versus Connection-Oriented
sections.content:
The prime reason SNMP uses connectionless transport is that it must keep working when the network is at its worst. For Telnet or FTP a user can try again later, but a management protocol exists to fix a network that is performing poorly. With UDP, only the sender of a request (typically the management station) needs timeouts and retransmission, which vastly reduces what an agent must do, since it only generates responses.

A connection-oriented transport forces a choice: keep a connection open to every managed object, set up and tear down per operation, or keep a fixed number open and swap them by an algorithm such as LRU. All three cause severe problems. Per-operation TCP use needs 10 separate packet transfers plus the TCP Time-Wait. A transport acknowledgment does not prove delivery to the application, and TCP flow control is not needed for lock-step SNMP exchanges.

The memo notes that purists may object to an application doing timeouts and retransmissions, but argues that a management application is best placed to adapt to the state of the network.
sections.plainLanguage: A phone call must be set up and kept going, which is hard on a bad line. A quick postcard just gets sent again if no reply comes, which is better when things break.

sections.title: Which Protocol to Choose
sections.content:
If a device is destined for use in the Internet, it must operate SNMP over UDP/IP. If it operates in another protocol environment, SNMP ought to use that environment's native transport services, since introducing a new protocol stack for one service can mean running and administering two stacks. The memo says the experimental standards for IPX and OSI ought to be followed in those environments.

The Security Considerations section says only that security issues are not discussed. An appendix lists the packets of one TCP-based SNMP operation: SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK, the request, the response with ACK, an ACK, then FIN, ACK, FIN-ACK and a last ACK.
sections.plainLanguage: On the Internet, use UDP. In other kinds of networks, use whatever that network already uses.
